replacement: Now and then he took his eyes off the newspaper and looked around. There was more noise than ever over at the house. The main building was called “the house” to tell it apart from the cottages. The chattering and whistling birds were still going. Two young girls, the Farival twins, were playing a duet from “Zampa” on the piano. Madame Lebrun bustled in and out. Whenever she was inside the house she gave orders in a high voice to a yard-boy, and whenever she was outside she gave directions in an equally high voice to a dining-room servant. She was a fresh, pretty woman, always dressed in white with elbow sleeves, and her starched skirts crinkled as she came and went. Farther down, in front of one of the cottages, a lady in black walked demurely up and down, telling her beads. A good many of the guests at the pension had crossed over to the Chênière Caminada in Beaudelet’s lugger to hear mass. Some young people were out under the water-oaks, playing croquet. Mr. Pontellier’s two children were there, sturdy little fellows of four and five, and a quadroon nurse followed them about with a faraway, meditative air.
“What folly, to go bathing at such an hour, in such heat!” exclaimed Mr. Pontellier. He himself had taken a plunge at daylight, and that was why the morning seemed so long to him.

“Will you be back for dinner?” his wife called. He stopped a moment and shrugged. He felt in his vest pocket, where a ten-dollar bill lay. He could not say. Maybe he would be back for the early dinner, and maybe not; it all hung on the company he found at Klein’s and the stakes of “the game.” He did not say so, but she understood, and she laughed and nodded him good-by.

“Could anyone fathom the cruelty under that fair exterior?” Robert murmured. “She knew I once adored her, and she let me. It was ‘Robert, come; go; stand up; sit down; do this; do that; see whether the baby sleeps; my thimble, please, which I left God knows where. Come and read Daudet to me while I sew.’”
“Blagueur — farceur — gros bête, va!”
“Mais ce n’est pas mal! Elle s’y connaît, elle a de la force, oui.”

Madame Lebrun was hard at work at the sewing-machine. A little black girl sat on the floor and worked the treadle with her hands. The Creole woman takes no chances with her health that can be avoided.
“Where is Victor going with the carriage?”
“The carriage? Victor?”
The little Black girl who ran Madame Lebrun’s sewing-machine was sweeping the galleries, with long, absent-minded strokes of the broom. Edna sent her up to the house to wake Robert.
“Tell him I am going to the Chêniere. The boat is ready; tell him to hurry.”
Edna liked it all. She looked Mariequita up and down, from her rough brown toes to her pretty black eyes, and back again.
All of them climbed together to the quaint little Gothic church of Our Lady of Lourdes, which gleamed brown and yellow with paint in the glare of the sun.
“All but the hundred years when you were sleeping. Good night.”
“At ten,” he said. “Beaudelet wants to wait for the moon.”
“No,” said Edna, a little sullenly. “I can’t be bothered dressing again; I don’t feel like it.”
“Don’t let us part in bad feeling. I’ve never known you to be out of patience with me before.”
“I will, thank you. Goodbye.”
Mademoiselle laughed, not kindly.
“Mariequita — yes, that was it; Mariequita. I had forgotten. Oh, she’s a sly one, and a bad one, that Mariequita!”
“Oh! I don’t know. Leave me alone—you bother me.”
“Yes, your friend Robert. He wrote to me from Mexico City.”
“Very well; Thursday. My wife may possibly have some engagement for me that night. If she has, I’ll send word. If not, expect me.”
“What a pity that so much talent has been neglected! But I must go.”

The moments glided on. Good fellowship passed around the circle like a mystic cord, and held these people together with jest and laughter. Monsieur Ratignolle was the first to break the pleasant charm. He excused himself at ten o’clock, since Madame Ratignolle was waiting for him at home. She was bien souffrante and full of vague dread, and only her husband’s presence could calm it.
“‘There was a graven image of Desire / Painted with red blood on a ground of gold.’”
“Ah! si tu savais / Ce que tes yeux me disent”—

Mr. Pontellier heard that his wife intended to abandon her home and set up house elsewhere. He answered at once with a letter of unqualified disapproval and remonstrance. She had given reasons that he was unwilling to acknowledge as adequate. He hoped she had not yet acted on her rash impulse, and he begged her to consider first, foremost and above all else what people would say. In warning her he was not dreaming of scandal, which would never have crossed his mind in connection with his wife’s name or his own. He was thinking simply of his financial integrity. Word might get around that the Pontelliers had met with reverses and had to run their ménage on a humbler scale than before. That might do incalculable mischief to his business prospects.

“Well, the reason is — you know how evil-minded the world can be — someone was talking about Alcée Arobin coming to see you. Of course it wouldn’t matter if Mr. Arobin didn’t have such a dreadful reputation. Monsieur Ratignolle was telling me that his attentions alone are considered enough to ruin a woman’s name.”
He came and took her hand, seemingly without knowing what he was saying or doing.

The dining room was very small. Edna’s round mahogany table would almost have filled it. As it was, the little table stood just a step or two from the kitchen, the mantel, the small buffet and the side door that opened onto the narrow, brick-paved yard.
“I’m not going to Mrs. Merriman’s,” she said. “If you see her, say so. But perhaps I had better write. I’ll do it now. I’ll say I’m sorry her child is ill, and that she shouldn’t count on me.”
“I’m destined to see you only by accident,” she said, pushing the cat off the chair next to her. He was startled, uneasy, almost embarrassed to meet her like this.

“She’ll bring you a plate, and you will share my dinner. There’s always enough for two, even three.” Edna had meant to be as indifferent and reserved as he was when she met him. She had reached that decision through a laborious train of reasoning, in one of her despondent moods. But her resolve melted when she saw him, whom a designing Providence had led into her path.

Edna walked on down to the beach rather mechanically. She noticed nothing special, except that the sun was hot, and she followed no particular train of thought. All the thinking she needed to do had been done after Robert went away, while she lay awake on the sofa until morning.
